children.text: Cuban-American members of Congress, including Florida Representative Illeana Ros-Lehtinen and Lincoln Diaz-Balart, held a press conference attacking NAFTA opponents' characterizations of Mexico's government and expressing alarm over signals that the Clinton administration might be quietly negotiating with Cuba. They demanded specifics on any talks and called on Clinton to consider an oil embargo against Cuba similar to the one imposed on Haiti. In Arizona, a U.S. Border Patrol agent was charged with kidnapping and raping an undocumented Mexican woman after arresting her near Nogales. The incident followed a string of documented human rights violations against Mexican nationals along the border, prompting Arizona Congressman Ed Pastor to introduce legislation creating an independent commission to investigate such abuses. An Urban Institute report challenged a widely cited Los Angeles County study that had claimed immigrants were a major drain on local government services. In Washington, the National Cancer Institute launched the first-ever in-depth cancer study of the D.C. Latino community, beginning with the Salvadoran population. Researchers were pleasantly surprised by high participation rates despite concerns that undocumented residents might be reluctant to engage. A Census Bureau report also noted that 39% of Latino/a births in 1991 were to unmarried women.
La Marqueta: East Harlem's Fading Marketplace

Correspondent Mandalit del Barco reported on La Marqueta, the historic East Harlem marketplace created in 1936 by Mayor Fiorello La Guardia to house pushcart vendors. Once a thriving hub of Puerto Rican commerce with five buildings and hundreds of vendors, La Marqueta had dwindled to a single building with eight or nine remaining merchants. The city's Economic Development Corporation committed $5 million to renovate the space and attract new tenants. City Council member Adam Clayton Powell IV envisioned a tourist-friendly flea market and affordable neighborhood shopping center, while his rival William Del Toro questioned spending $100,000 per vendor stall. Longtime butcher Alex Garcet, who had laid off 11 employees but refused to leave, said he stayed out of hope that La Marqueta would one day return to its former vitality.

Maria Hinojosa spoke with San Diego artist and immigrant rights activist David Avalos about Arte Reembolso, a project in which he and collaborators Lewis Hawk and Elizabeth Cisco distributed $10 bills marked with messages about the economic contributions of undocumented workers to day laborers in the San Diego area. The National Endowment for the Arts withdrew its funding after the project generated public outrage. Avalos argued the reaction was entirely out of proportion to the $1,250 the NEA had contributed, and that the project simply made visible what politicians and media had obscured: that undocumented immigrants pay taxes through payroll deductions, gas purchases, and retail spending, and are legitimate members of the tax-paying community.

Correspondent Catalina Reyes reported from the Museum of International Folk Art in Santa Fe on an exhibition titled The Art of the Santera, featuring the work of 26 women practitioners of New Mexico's 400-year-old tradition of carving and painting wooden images of Catholic saints. Curator Helen Lucero explained that while the tradition had been exclusively male in its public form, women had long been the keepers of faith in New Mexico homes. The exhibit broadened the definition of santera to include work in tin, embroidery, weaving, hide painting, and ceramics. A highlight was a carving of Santa Librada, the only crucified woman saint, whom legend says prayed for God to make her unattractive to prevent an unwanted marriage and who historically served as an intercessor for women with difficult husbands. Lucero noted that many of the featured artists described their work as deeply spiritual, seeing themselves as bridges between the sacred and the everyday.

To mark the start of Hispanic Heritage Month, Latino USA aired remarks from past honorees at Washington's annual celebration of Latino/a contributions to American life. Puerto Rican educator Dr. Antonia Pantoja, founder of ASPIRA and the National Puerto Rican Forum, spoke from her home in the mountains of Puerto Rico about the importance of community, family, and acknowledging Afro-Latina identity. Playwright Luis Valdez, founder of El Teatro Campesino and recognized as the father of modern Chicano theater, delivered a wide-ranging address tracing Indigenous names for the Americas and arguing that Latino/a people carried within their history and their bloodlines a vision of cultural unity that the Anglo world had yet to fully understand.
